questions.question: Differentiate between simple interest and compound interest with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Simple Interest and Compound Interest are two methods of calculating the return on a loan or
  • investment. Simple Interest is calculated only on the original principal amount throughout the entire
  • period. For example, if ₹10,000 is invested at 10% annual interest for two years, the simple interest
  • earned will be ₹2,000, and the total amount becomes ₹12,000. In contrast, Compound Interest is
  • calculated on the principal as well as on the accumulated interest from previous periods. Using the same
  • example, the compound interest after two years would be ₹2,100, making the total amount ₹12,100.
  • Thus, compound interest grows faster than simple interest because it allows interest to earn further
  • interest over time
questions.final_answer: interest over time
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Differentiate between a Column Chart and a Bar Chart.
questions.solution_html:
• A Column Chart and a Bar Chart are both used to compare data, but they differ mainly in orientation
  • and purpose. A Column Chart displays data using vertical bars, with categories placed along the
  • horizontal axis and values along the vertical axis. It is especially useful for showing changes or trends
  • over time, such as monthly sales or yearly growth. In contrast, a Bar Chart uses horizontal bars, with
  • categories on the vertical axis and values on the horizontal axis. Bar charts are more effective when
  • comparing different categories or when category names are long, such as comparing sales performance
questions.final_answer: comparing different categories or when category names are long, such as comparing sales performance
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the procedure to calculate coefficient of variation Excel.
questions.solution_html:
• Steps in Excel: to find coefficient of variation
  • • Enter your data in a column (for example, cells A1:A10).
  • • Calculate the Mean
  • =AVERAGE(A1:A10)
  • • Calculate the Standard Deviation (Sample)
  • =STDEV.S(A1:A10)
  • (Use STDEV.P if the data represents a population.)
  • • Calculate the Coefficient of Variation
  • =(STDEV.S(A1:A10)/AVERAGE(A1:A10))*100
  • • Press Enter — Excel will display the CV as a percentage.
questions.final_answer: • Press Enter — Excel will display the CV as a percentage

questions.question: What is non linear regression model?
questions.solution_html:
• A non-linear regression model is a type of regression analysis in which the relationship between
  • the independent variable(s) and the dependent variable is not a straight line. Unlike linear regression
  • which involves a simple linear equation, non-linear regression involves curved relationships that
  • cannot be represented by a simple linear equation. A non-linear regression model is one where the
  • change in the dependent variable does not occur at a constant rate with changes in the independent
  • variable. The parameters appear in a non-linear form.
questions.final_answer: variable. The parameters appear in a non-linear form

questions.question: “Explain the concept and importance of a Scattergram (XY Scatter Plot) in data analysis. How does the CORREL() function in Excel complement the interpretation of a scattergram?
questions.solution_html:
• A scattergram (or scatter plot) is a graphical tool used to display the relationship between two
  • quantitative variables. Each point on the chart represents a pair of values — one from each variable —
  • allowing patterns, trends, and relationships to be visually identified.
  • Concept: In a scattergram, the independent variable (X) is plotted on the horizontal axis, and the
  • dependent variable (Y) is plotted on the vertical axis. The pattern formed by the points indicates the
  • type of relationship
  • • Upward sloping: Positive correlation (as X increases, Y increases).
  • • Downward sloping: Negative correlation (as X increases, Y decreases).
  • • Scattered randomly: No correlation.
  • Importance
questions.final_answer: Importance
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the difference between FIND() and SEARCH() with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• The FIND() and SEARCH() functions in Excel are both used to locate the position of a specific
  • character or substring within a text, but they differ in how they handle case and wildcards. The FIND()
  • function is case-sensitive, meaning it distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters, and it does
  • not support wildcard characters. For example, =FIND("A","Apple") returns 1, while
  • =FIND("a","Apple") gives an error because the lowercase “a” is treated differently. In contrast, the
  • SEARCH() function is not case-sensitive and supports wildcards, making it more flexible. For instance
  • =SEARCH("a","Apple") also returns 1, and =SEARCH("p*","Apple") works because of wildcard
  • support. In short, FIND() is stricter, while SEARCH() is more forgiving and versatile for text searches.
questions.final_answer: support. In short, FIND() is stricter, while SEARCH() is more forgiving and versatile for text searches

questions.question: Explain how IRR is used as a tool for evaluating mutually exclusive projects. Discuss the multiple IRR problem with an example
questions.solution_html:
• (Liberal Valuation).
  • The Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is a financial tool used to evaluate the profitability of investment
  • projects. It represents the discount rate at which the Net Present Value (NPV) of a project’s cash flows
  • becomes zero. In simpler terms, IRR is the rate of return that makes the project break even in present
  • value terms.
  • Evaluating Mutually Exclusive Projects
  • When two or more projects are mutually exclusive (i.e., only one can be chosen), IRR helps compare
  • their potential returns.
  • • A higher IRR generally indicates a more profitable project, provided other factors like project
  • size and timing are similar.
  • • However, IRR should be used along with NPV, as IRR alone can sometimes give misleading
  • results — especially when cash flows differ significantly in timing or scale.
  • The Multiple IRR Problem: The multiple IRR problem occurs when a project has non-conventional
  • cash flows, meaning the signs of cash flows change more than once (for example, from positive to
  • negative and back to positive).
  • Each change in sign can result in a different IRR value, making it unclear which rate is the correct one
  • for decision-making.
  • (5x3=(15 marks))

questions.question: Differentiate between simple interest and compound interest with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Simple Interest and Compound Interest are two methods of calculating the return on a loan or
  • investment. Simple Interest is calculated only on the original principal amount throughout the entire
  • period. For example, if ₹10,000 is invested at 10% annual interest for two years, the simple interest
  • earned will be ₹2,000, and the total amount becomes ₹12,000. In contrast, Compound Interest is
  • calculated on the principal as well as on the accumulated interest from previous periods. Using the same
  • example, the compound interest after two years would be ₹2,100, making the total amount ₹12,100.
  • Thus, compound interest grows faster than simple interest because it allows interest to earn further
  • interest over time
questions.final_answer: interest over time

questions.question: Differentiate between a Column Chart and a Bar Chart.
questions.solution_html:
• A Column Chart and a Bar Chart are both used to compare data, but they differ mainly in orientation
  • and purpose. A Column Chart displays data using vertical bars, with categories placed along the
  • horizontal axis and values along the vertical axis. It is especially useful for showing changes or trends
  • over time, such as monthly sales or yearly growth. In contrast, a Bar Chart uses horizontal bars, with
  • categories on the vertical axis and values on the horizontal axis. Bar charts are more effective when
  • comparing different categories or when category names are long, such as comparing sales performance
questions.final_answer: comparing different categories or when category names are long, such as comparing sales performance

questions.question: Explain the procedure to calculate coefficient of variation Excel.
questions.solution_html:
• Steps in Excel: to find coefficient of variation
  • • Enter your data in a column (for example, cells A1:A10).
  • • Calculate the Mean
  • =AVERAGE(A1:A10)
  • • Calculate the Standard Deviation (Sample)
  • =STDEV.S(A1:A10)
  • (Use STDEV.P if the data represents a population.)
  • • Calculate the Coefficient of Variation
  • =(STDEV.S(A1:A10)/AVERAGE(A1:A10))*100
  • • Press Enter — Excel will display the CV as a percentage.
questions.final_answer: • Press Enter — Excel will display the CV as a percentage

questions.question: What is non linear regression model?
questions.solution_html:
• A non-linear regression model is a type of regression analysis in which the relationship between
  • the independent variable(s) and the dependent variable is not a straight line. Unlike linear regression

  • cannot be represented by a simple linear equation. A non-linear regression model is one where the
  • change in the dependent variable does not occur at a constant rate with changes in the independent
  • variable. The parameters appear in a non-linear form.

  • dependent variable (Y) is plotted on the vertical axis. The pattern formed by the points indicates the
  • type of relationship
  • • Upward sloping: Positive correlation (as X increases, Y increases).

questions.question: Explain the difference between FIND() and SEARCH() with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• The FIND() and SEARCH() functions in Excel are both used to locate the position of a specific
  • character or substring within a text, but they differ in how they handle case and wildcards. The FIND()
  • function is case-sensitive, meaning it distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters, and it does
  • not support wildcard characters. For example, =FIND("A","Apple") returns 1, while
  • =FIND("a","Apple") gives an error because the lowercase “a” is treated differently. In contrast, the
  • SEARCH() function is not case-sensitive and supports wildcards, making it more flexible. For instance
  • =SEARCH("a","Apple") also returns 1, and =SEARCH("p*","Apple") works because of wildcard
  • support. In short, FIND() is stricter, while SEARCH() is more forgiving and versatile for text searches.
questions.final_answer: support. In short, FIND() is stricter, while SEARCH() is more forgiving and versatile for text searches

questions.question: Explain how IRR is used as a tool for evaluating mutually exclusive projects. Discuss the multiple IRR problem with an example
questions.solution_html:
• (Liberal Valuation).
  • The Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is a financial tool used to evaluate the profitability of investment
  • projects. It represents the discount rate at which the Net Present Value (NPV) of a project’s cash flows
  • becomes zero. In simpler terms, IRR is the rate of return that makes the project break even in present
  • value terms.
  • Evaluating Mutually Exclusive Projects
  • When two or more projects are mutually exclusive (i.e., only one can be chosen), IRR helps compare
  • their potential returns.
  • • A higher IRR generally indicates a more profitable project, provided other factors like project
  • size and timing are similar.
  • • However, IRR should be used along with NPV, as IRR alone can sometimes give misleading
  • results — especially when cash flows differ significantly in timing or scale.
  • The Multiple IRR Problem: The multiple IRR problem occurs when a project has non-conventional
  • cash flows, meaning the signs of cash flows change more than once (for example, from positive to
  • negative and back to positive).
  • Each change in sign can result in a different IRR value, making it unclear which rate is the correct one
  • for decision-making.
